items.meaningEn: very interested in or enthusiastic about something
items.why: Q1 asks what The Junction is especially good for. The table uses “keen on”, so you listen for an activity or interest, not for a price or location.
items.example: The Junction — Greyson Street, near the station — especially good for people who are keen on ______ — quite expensive — the ______ is a good place for a drink

items.meaningEn: money paid in advance to reserve something
items.why: The Paloma entry mentions a £50 deposit. Knowing that a deposit is an upfront payment stops you confusing it with the total bill or the per-person price.
items.example: Paloma — in Bow Street, next to the cinema — ______ food, good for sharing — staff very friendly — £50 deposit — a limited selection of ______ food on the menu

items.meaningEn: a meal at a fixed price, usually served at lunchtime
items.meaningVi: suất ăn trưa giá cố định
items.why: Q9 asks for the cost of the set lunch. “Set” means the meal has a fixed price, so you listen for the price attached to that meal rather than individual dishes.
items.example: The ______ — at the top of a ______ — a famous chef — all the ______ are very good — only uses ______ ingredients — set lunch costs £______ per person — portions of ______ size

items.meaningEn: the amount of food served to one person
items.why: Q10 asks about the size of the portions. “Portion” means the amount served to one person, so you listen for a size word rather than a price or ingredient.
items.example: The ______ — at the top of a ______ — a famous chef — all the ______ are very good — only uses ______ ingredients — set lunch costs £______ per person — portions of ______ size

items.meaningEn: to live or last longer than something else
items.meaningVi: sống lâu hơn; tồn tại lâu hơn
items.why: Q13 asks why some people join the class. “Outlive” means to last longer than the maker, so it points to the idea of leaving something behind.
items.example: make something that will outlive them.

items.meaningEn: a quality that makes someone feel relaxed
items.why: Q14 asks what Heather values most. “Calming effect” is a paraphrase of feeling relaxed or stress-free, so it helps you reject the messy or physical-benefit options.
items.example: Heather values pottery’s calming effect.

items.meaningEn: completely necessary
items.why: Q19–20 ask about a potter’s tools. “Essential items” means tools that cannot be done without, a common paraphrase of “necessary”.
items.example: Some tools are essential items for a potter.

items.meaningEn: a piece of clothing worn to protect the front of your clothes
items.why: Q16 reminds visitors what to do before starting. An apron protects clothing, so the word helps you identify the practical preparation step rather than a clothing change.
items.example: Visitors should put on their aprons before starting.

items.meaningEn: a condition that causes memory loss and mental decline
items.why: Q23–24 ask which health risks are supported by solid evidence. “Dementia” is a specific medical condition, so you need to hear it named rather than accept a vague health claim.
items.example: Dementia is one of the health risks linked to loneliness.

items.meaningEn: relating to the heart and blood vessels
items.why: Q23–24 include cardiovascular disease as a health risk. Knowing the word helps you recognise it when the recording talks about the heart or circulation.
items.example: Cardiovascular disease affects the heart and blood vessels.

items.meaningEn: described as greater or more important than it really is
items.why: Q27 contrasts a medical cure with the claim that the link between loneliness and mental health is overstated. The word signals that the speaker thinks the link is exaggerated.
items.example: claim that the link between loneliness and mental health is overstated.

items.meaningEn: the state of being alone
items.meaningVi: sự ở một mình; sự cô độc
items.why: Q30 asks why solitude is considered enjoyable. The word means being alone, which the students find different from loneliness, so it helps you follow the distinction.
items.example: The students find it difficult to understand why solitude is considered to be

items.meaningEn: waste water and waste matter carried away in drains
items.meaningVi: nước thải; chất thải sinh hoạt
items.why: Q31 asks for the source of pollution on the river bank. “Sewage” is a common cause of river pollution, so it helps you listen for waste rather than industry or farming.
items.example: Industrial development and rising populations led to more sewage and pollution from ______ on the river bank.

items.meaningEn: so polluted that almost no life can survive
items.why: Q32 asks what the Thames was declared in 1957. The phrase means the river could no longer support living organisms, a stronger claim than simply “polluted”.
items.example: In 1957, the River Thames was declared biologically ______.

items.meaningEn: a flat boat used to carry goods
items.why: Q39 asks about electric vehicles that could transport goods. “Freight” means goods carried in bulk, and a barge is a river boat, so the phrase points to goods transport by water.
items.example: Goods could travel by freight barges and electric ______, or in future by ______.

items.meaningEn: a large building used for storing goods
items.why: Q34 asks what riverside warehouses are converted into. The word means a storage building, so it helps you understand the redevelopment of old industrial riverside sites.
items.example: Riverside warehouses are converted into restaurants and ______.

items.meaningEn: the state of not being able to do something
items.why: Q1 asks whether other parrots share the kākāpō’s inability to fly. The word turns the statement into a comparison of flying ability, which you must check in the passage.
items.example: There are other parrots that share the kākāpō's inability to fly.

items.meaningEn: living wild after escaping from domestication
items.meaningVi: hoang dã; đã thoát khỏi nuôi nhốt
items.why: Q5 asks why kākāpō were moved from Rakiura. “Feral cats” means wild cats, not domestic pets, so the word helps you identify the threat described.
items.example: Kākāpō were transferred from Rakiura Island to other locations because they were at risk from feral cats.

items.meaningEn: at extremely high risk of extinction
items.why: The subtitle describes the kākāpō as critically endangered. This tells you the passage is about a species close to extinction and helps you interpret population figures and conservation efforts.
items.example: The kākāpō is a nocturnal, flightless parrot that is critically endangered.

items.meaningEn: a plan or programme designed to solve a problem
items.meaningVi: sáng kiến; chương trình hành động
items.why: Q6 asks about a Recovery Plan initiative. “Initiative” means an organised scheme, so you look for a specific action within the plan rather than a general aim.
items.example: One Recovery Plan initiative that helped increase the kākāpō population size was caring for struggling young birds.

items.meaningEn: active at night
items.why: The subtitle describes the kākāpō as nocturnal. The word means active at night, a key fact about its behaviour and a likely focus in the passage.
items.example: The kākāpō is a nocturnal, flightless parrot.

items.meaningEn: the protection of wildlife and natural places
items.why: The passage describes conservation efforts to save the kākāpō. The word helps you identify actions taken to protect the species rather than explain its biology.
items.example: Conservationist Richard Henry led an effort to relocate several hundred of the birds.

items.meaningEn: to bring a species or thing back to a place where it once existed
items.meaningVi: đưa trở lại; tái du nhập
items.why: Q15–16 concern attempts to reintroduce elms. The word means bringing the tree back, not simply protecting the few trees that remain.
items.example: details of a difference of opinion about the value of reintroducing elms to Britain

items.meaningEn: able to withstand disease or damage
items.why: Q19–23 discuss trees that survive Dutch elm disease. “Resistant” describes trees that can fight the disease, a key distinction from trees that are merely old.
items.example: Growers look for elm trees that are resistant to Dutch elm disease.

items.meaningEn: important, noticeable, or widespread
items.meaningVi: nổi bật; phổ biến; đáng chú ý
items.why: Q23 asks about the effect of seeing how prominent the elm once was. The word means the tree was a striking feature of the landscape, not just that it existed.
items.example: You understand the effect Dutch elm disease has had when you see evidence of how prominent the tree once was.

items.meaningEn: easily harmed or attacked
items.why: Q18 asks when young elms become vulnerable. The word signals the stage at which they can be attacked by disease, so you look for a change in their ability to survive.
items.example: reference to the stage at which young elms become vulnerable to Dutch elm disease

items.meaningEn: fully grown or developed
items.meaningVi: trưởng thành; đã phát triển đầy đủ
items.why: Q20 refers to mature elms that have survived. The word means fully grown trees, so it helps you distinguish older survivors from young seedlings.
items.example: It may be better to wait and see if the mature elms that have survived continue to flourish.

items.meaningEn: a belief accepted by many people, often without proof
items.meaningVi: giả định được nhiều người tin
items.why: Q27 asks how the writer introduces the topic. The phrase signals that the writer will question a belief many people share, a common introduction technique.
items.example: questioning a widely held assumption.

items.meaningEn: the methods used in a piece of research
items.why: Q29 asks what the writer is doing in the fourth paragraph. “Methodology” is the set of methods used, so it helps you distinguish a description of procedure from findings or objectives.
items.example: The writer describes the study’s methodology.

items.meaningEn: an increased ability to notice or react to something
items.why: Q30 asks about a brain mechanism. The phrase means people become more alert to signals of threat, not that they become better at controlling anxiety.
items.example: produces heightened sensitivity to indications of external threats.

items.meaningEn: an action taken to prevent danger or problems
items.why: Q39 asks whether stress can lead us to take unnecessary precautions. The word means actions taken to avoid a risk, which may be unnecessary if the risk is exaggerated.
items.example: Stress created by social media posts can lead us to take unnecessary precautions.

items.meaningEn: a hormone released by the body under stress
items.why: Q34 mentions cortisol levels and heart rates. The word names a stress hormone, so it helps you understand the physical response being measured.
items.example: The students' cortisol levels and heart rates were affected when the researchers

items.meaningEn: a person who looks after someone who is ill, old, or disabled
items.why: The whole table is about practical support for carers. Knowing that a carer looks after a relative helps you follow who needs help and what kind of support is being discussed.
items.example: # Practical support for carers

items.meaningEn: an official judgement of someone’s needs or abilities
items.why: The table asks what an assessment of the mother’s needs may include. “Assessment” signals a structured review, so you listen for categories of need rather than a single task.
items.example: ## Assessment of mother's needs

items.meaningEn: duties or tasks that someone must deal with
items.why: Q1 asks what the carer can have time for. “Other responsibilities” means other duties, so you listen for something the carer cannot do while caring.
items.example: time for other responsibilities — a ______

items.meaningEn: a substance burned to produce power, especially for vehicles
items.why: Q9 asks for a car-related cost besides fuel. The word means the energy source for a car, so it helps you identify another running cost rather than a repair.
items.example: car-related costs, e.g. fuel and ______

items.meaningEn: attention given to something by the media or public
items.meaningVi: sự quảng bá; sự chú ý của công chúng
items.why: Q14 asks about helping with a magazine. “Providing publicity about a council service” means promoting it to the public, so you listen for marketing or information work.
items.example: Oat milk: a Swedish brand's media campaign received publicity by upsetting competitors; promotion in the USA through ______ shops reduced the need for advertising; it appealed to consumers concerned about the ______.

items.meaningEn: the ability to communicate and work well with people
items.why: Q18 asks for the most important requirement for volunteers. “Interpersonal skills” means getting on with people, so it helps you choose between interest and flexibility.
items.example: Volunteers need strong interpersonal skills.

items.meaningEn: the ability to change plans or adapt to different situations
items.why: Q18 includes flexibility as a possible requirement. It means being able to change when needed, which is different from simply being interested in the event.
items.example: Flexibility is one of the requirements for festival volunteers.

items.meaningEn: the act of working together
items.why: One volunteer role is encouraging cooperation between local organisations. The word means getting groups to work together, so it helps you distinguish it from providing information or selling tickets.
items.example: H encouraging cooperation between local organisations

items.meaningEn: not clear or precise
items.why: Q21–25 ask for opinions on aspects of human geography. “The information was too vague” means it lacked detail, so it helps you reject an option that says the information was useful.
items.example: A The information given about this was too vague.

items.meaningEn: able to be trusted or depended on
items.why: Q21–25 include the idea that facts may not be reliable. The word signals a doubt about accuracy, which is different from saying the topic is irrelevant or interesting.
items.example: E The facts about this may not be reliable.

items.meaningEn: no longer used
items.why: Q28 asks about developing disused industrial sites. “Disused” means the sites are no longer in use, so you listen for the costs or benefits of redeveloping them.
items.example: The students agree that developing disused industrial sites may

items.meaningEn: the areas at the edge of a city
items.meaningVi: vùng ngoại vi; rìa thành phố
items.why: Q27 asks about recent additions to the outskirts of their cities. The word means the outer edge of a city, so it helps you locate new facilities outside the centre.
items.example: What recent additions to the outskirts of their cities are both students happy about?

items.meaningEn: a social media user who can affect what others buy
items.meaningVi: người có ảnh hưởng trên mạng
items.why: The notes mention influencers becoming brand ambassadors. Knowing the term helps you follow how social media users promote food brands and drive sales.
items.example: Influencers on social media become brand ambassadors.

items.meaningEn: a person paid or chosen to represent a brand
items.why: The notes describe influencers becoming brand ambassadors. The phrase means they officially represent a brand, not just mention it once.
items.example: Influencers on social media become brand ambassadors.

items.meaningEn: the use of something too much or too often
items.why: Q40 asks what overuse of resources did to quinoa quality. “Overuse” means using land or resources beyond a sustainable level, which explains the fall in quality.
items.example: Quinoa: its success led to an increase in its ______; overuse of resources resulted in poor quality ______.

items.meaningEn: the amount of a product that people want to buy
items.why: The notes say supermarkets track demand for ingredients. The word means how much people want to buy, so it helps you understand how social media trends affect sales.
items.example: Supermarkets track demand for ingredients on social media.

items.meaningEn: living in or connected with water
items.why: Q7 asks whether West Indian manatees live in a variety of aquatic habitats. “Aquatic” tells you the habitats are in water, so you check for different water environments, not land ones.
items.example: West Indian manatees can be found in a variety of different aquatic habitats.

items.meaningEn: the state of being caught or twisted in something
items.why: Q12 asks about entanglement and plastic consumption. “Entanglement” means being caught in fishing nets, a specific risk that is different from eating plastic.
items.example: The risk to manatees from entanglement and plastic consumption increased significantly in the period 2009–2020.

items.meaningEn: laws made by a government
items.why: Q13 asks whether legislation aims to reduce boat strikes. The word means official laws, so you check for a legal measure rather than a voluntary guideline.
items.example: There is some legislation in place which aims to reduce the likelihood of boat strikes on manatees in Florida.

items.meaningEn: the chance that something will happen
items.why: Q13 refers to reducing the likelihood of boat strikes. The word means the chance of an event, so you look for a measure that makes strikes less probable.
items.example: There is some legislation in place which aims to reduce the likelihood of boat strikes on manatees in Florida.

items.meaningEn: the natural environment where an animal lives
items.why: Q7 asks about aquatic habitats. The word means the places where manatees naturally live, so it helps you check whether they use a range of water environments.
items.example: West Indian manatees can be found in a variety of different aquatic habitats.

items.meaningEn: the habit of delaying tasks that need to be done
items.why: The passage explains why we put off important tasks. “Procrastination” is the key concept, so you need it to follow the causes, consequences and advice.
items.example: neurological evidence of a link between procrastination and emotion

items.meaningEn: a belief that is wrong but accepted without proof
items.why: Q14 asks for a mention of false assumptions about why people procrastinate. The phrase signals a belief the passage will correct, so you look for a contrast with the real cause.
items.example: mention of false assumptions about why people procrastinate

items.meaningEn: relating to the brain and nervous system
items.why: Q16 asks for neurological evidence linking procrastination and emotion. The word tells you the evidence comes from brain activity, not from surveys or interviews.
items.example: neurological evidence of a link between procrastination and emotion

items.meaningEn: easy enough to deal with or achieve
items.why: Q25–26 ask for recommendations. “Manageable aims” means goals that are realistic, so you listen for advice to make tasks smaller rather than to work harder.
items.example: The writer recommends setting manageable aims.

items.meaningEn: a strong feeling such as fear, anger, or happiness
items.why: Q16 asks for neurological evidence linking procrastination and emotion. The word signals a role for feelings, which helps you distinguish emotional explanations from time-management ones.
items.example: neurological evidence of a link between procrastination and emotion

items.meaningEn: to change something slightly, usually a rule or document
items.why: Q28 asks whether MLB amended the size of the strike zone. “Amend” means to make a formal change, so you check whether the rule itself was altered.
items.example: MLB considered it necessary to amend the size of the strike zone when criticisms were received from players.

items.meaningEn: possible to do successfully
items.why: Q32 asks whether ABS makes changes to the strike zone feasible. The word means possible to carry out, so it helps you distinguish a practical effect from a prediction.
items.example: ABS makes changes to the shape of the strike zone feasible.

items.meaningEn: based on personal opinion rather than fixed facts
items.why: Q33–37 include “subjective assessment” in the summary options. It contrasts with an objective, measured judgement, which is central to the passage’s argument about umpires.
items.example: Umpires make a subjective assessment of the strike zone.

items.meaningEn: noticed or understood in a particular way
items.meaningVi: được nhận thức; được cảm nhận
items.why: Q33–37 include “perceived area”. The word means the area as people experience or understand it, not necessarily its exact measured size.
items.example: The perceived area may differ from its measured size.

items.meaningEn: the quality of being correct or exact
items.why: Q29 and Q39 discuss the accuracy of ABS. The word means how exact the system is, so it helps you follow the trade-off between precision and enjoyment.
items.example: MLB is keen to justify the money spent on improving the accuracy of ABS's calculations.

items.meaningEn: an arrangement in which you pay to use something owned by someone else
items.meaningVi: sự thuê; dịch vụ cho thuê
items.why: The table compares furniture rental companies. “Rental” tells you the customer is paying to use furniture temporarily, not buying it outright.
items.example: The table compares furniture rental companies.

items.meaningEn: neither the cheapest nor the most expensive
items.why: The second company is described as mid-range. This helps you place it between the cheapest and most expensive options when comparing prices.
items.example: ______ and Oliver — mid-range prices — 12% monthly fee for ______ — also offers a cleaning service

items.meaningEn: a formal agreement, especially for a period of service
items.why: The table gives a minimum contract length of six months. “Contract” signals a formal rental agreement, so you listen for the time commitment rather than the price.
items.example: Larch Furniture — offers the cheapest prices for renting furniture and ______ items — must have own ______ — minimum contract length: six months

items.meaningEn: including the most recent information
items.why: Q9 asks where to see the most up-to-date prices. The phrase means the newest prices, so you look for a website or notice rather than an old brochure.
items.example: ______ Rentals — see the ______ for the most up-to-date prices — ______ are allowed within 7 days of delivery

items.meaningEn: relating to the study of past societies through their remains
items.why: The talk is about an archaeological dig. Knowing the word helps you follow the evidence, structures and objects being discussed as clues about the past.
items.example: The talk describes an archaeological dig at Bidcaster.

items.meaningEn: the parts of a building, object, or body left from the past
items.why: Q15 asks what was found on the other side of the river. “Remains” can mean the surviving parts of a building, so it helps you identify structural evidence rather than a complete building.
items.example: the remains of a large palace

items.meaningEn: the outer shape or boundary of something
items.why: Q15 includes “the outline of fields”. The word means the visible boundary or shape left in the ground, not the crops themselves.
items.example: The outline of fields was visible on the other side of the river.

items.meaningEn: a device used to find metal objects underground
items.why: Q12 asks how the gold coin was found. A metal detector is a device for locating metal, so the phrase helps you identify the method rather than the cause of soil removal.
items.example: A person with a metal detector searched the area.

items.meaningEn: a belief that is wrong
items.why: Q22 asks about a mistaken belief about theatre programmes. The phrase signals that the speaker will correct a common but false idea.
items.example: Maya says a mistaken belief about theatre programmes is that

items.meaningEn: costing nothing
items.why: Q23 asks about early British theatre programmes. “Free of charge” means audiences did not pay for them, so it helps you reject the idea that they were difficult to obtain.
items.example: were given out free of charge.

items.meaningEn: providing useful or interesting information
items.meaningVi: cung cấp nhiều thông tin; bổ ích
items.why: Q25 compares eighteenth- and nineteenth-century programmes. “Informative” means they contained more useful information, not that they were more colourful or original.
items.example: Eighteenth-century programmes were more informative.

items.meaningEn: the people who watch or listen to a performance
items.why: Q23 asks whether early programmes were difficult for audiences to obtain. The word means the people watching the plays, so it helps you focus on theatre-goers rather than companies.
items.example: were difficult for audiences to obtain.

items.meaningEn: design that works for as many different people as possible
items.why: The whole lecture defines inclusive design. Knowing the term helps you understand that the aim is to remove barriers for diverse users rather than create special products.
items.example: Inclusive design removes barriers for a wide range of users.

items.meaningEn: able to be changed to suit different people or situations
items.why: Q33 asks about adjustable workplace items. The word means the item can be changed to fit the user, which is the key feature preventing back or neck problems.
items.example: ______ which are adjustable, avoiding back or neck problems

items.meaningEn: causing difficulty or being unsuitable
items.meaningVi: có vấn đề; gây khó khăn
items.why: Q37–40 discuss products that are problematic for women. The word signals a design failure, so you look for the specific group and reason.
items.example: Safety: seatbelts are especially problematic for ______ women; PPE jackets are often unsuitable because of the size of women's ______; PPE for female ______ officers dealing with emergencies is the worst.

items.meaningEn: the screen or controls through which a user operates a device
items.why: Q35–36 discuss colours and commands in interfaces. The word means the part of a device people interact with, so it helps you understand usability problems for older users.
items.example: To assist the elderly: designers avoid using ______ in interfaces; people can make commands using a mouse, keyboard or their ______.

items.meaningEn: the movement of goods or people from one place to another
items.why: Q8 concerns the ice transportation business. The word helps you understand that the passage is about moving ice, not producing or storing it.
items.example: The ice transportation business made some Boston ship owners very wealthy in the early 1800s.

items.meaningEn: a condition that makes something less useful or successful
items.why: Q9 asks about a disadvantage of the freezing process. The word signals a negative feature, so you look for a problem such as changed taste rather than a benefit.
items.example: A disadvantage of the freezing process invented in Australia was that it affected the taste of food.

items.meaningEn: activity intended to make a product more popular or known
items.why: Q11 asks about investment in the promotion of the TV Dinner. The word means marketing activity, so you listen for spending on advertising rather than on food production.
items.example: Swanson Foods invested a great deal of money in the promotion of the TV Dinner.

items.meaningEn: an object used to hold or pack something
items.why: Q12 asks about a new style of container. The word means the packaging that holds the meal, so it helps you focus on the physical design rather than the food itself.
items.example: Swanson Foods developed a new style of container for the launch of the TV Dinner.

items.meaningEn: the process of keeping food cold to preserve it
items.meaningVi: sự làm lạnh; bảo quản lạnh
items.why: Q? and the passage discuss refrigeration as the key to frozen food. The word means keeping food cold, so it helps you follow the development of the industry.
items.example: Refrigeration allows food to be kept cold for longer.

items.meaningEn: the presence of a harmful or unwanted substance
items.meaningVi: sự ô nhiễm; sự nhiễm bẩn
items.why: Q20–21 list contamination of the sea from waste as a cause of damage. The word means harmful substances entering the water, so it helps you distinguish pollution from overfishing or disease.
items.example: the contamination of the sea from waste

items.why: Q22–23 ask which corals can cope with changed sea conditions. The phrase means survive and function despite stress, so it helps you identify corals that are more resilient.
items.example: They are looking at corals that can cope well with the changed sea conditions.

items.meaningEn: the process by which living things produce young
items.why: Q22–23 mention methods that speed up reproduction. The word means the process of producing new corals, so it helps you distinguish breeding from protecting or moving them.
items.example: They are trying out methods that would speed up reproduction in some corals.

items.meaningEn: the process of returning something to a good condition
items.meaningVi: sự phục hồi; sự khôi phục
items.why: The passage discusses coral reef restoration. The word means actively repairing the reef, so it helps you distinguish restoration from mere protection.
items.example: Coral reef restoration is a major conservation goal.

items.meaningEn: to limit the size, amount, or freedom of something
items.why: Q27 says humans may need to restrict the abilities of robots. The word means to keep robot abilities within limits, a key safety proposal in the passage.
items.example: For our own safety, humans will need to restrict the abilities of robots.

items.meaningEn: relating to moral principles
items.why: Q34 asks about the ethical aspect of treating robots. The word signals a question of right and wrong, not simply practical usefulness.

items.meaningEn: a natural tendency to behave in a particular way
items.why: Q37 asks what point Richardson makes about fear of machines. Her explanation involves a human inclination to attribute human qualities to objects, so the word helps you follow her argument.
items.example: It is the result of our inclination to attribute human characteristics to non-human entities.
